name: Hotelling's Law
statement: Competitors tend to make their products as similar as possible, clustering in the middle of the market.
meaning: When rivals sell to customers spread across a market and each buyer picks the nearest option, each firm can grab a bigger share by edging toward its rival's position. Because both reason the same way, they end up clustered together at the centre instead of spreading out: near-identical offerings aimed at the middle.
mechanism: Picture two ice-cream sellers on a beach with customers spread evenly along it, each buying from the closer seller. Starting spread out, each seller realises it can capture some of the rival's customers by moving inward without losing the ones behind it, who still have no closer option. Both keep moving in, and the only stable resting point is back-to-back at the midpoint: worse for customers, who now walk further, but individually rational for each seller.

examples.text: Competing chains locate near one another (fast-food outlets at the same junction, rival pharmacies on opposite corners, big-box stores in the same retail park), each pulled toward the centre of demand rather than spreading out to serve it evenly.

Applied to politics by Anthony Downs, the same logic produces convergence on the median voter: two major parties edge toward the middle of the ideological line, ending up closer together than their bases.
Firms imitate rivals' features rather than offering genuinely distinct alternatives, yielding minimally differentiated goods clustered on the same shared attributes.

variants.name: The median voter theorem
variants.text: The political form, proved by Duncan Black and popularised by Anthony Downs (1957): under majority rule on a single dimension, outcomes converge on the median voter's preference.

variants.name: Maximum differentiation
variants.text: The opposite pole, which later models favour: to soften price competition, firms may move as far apart as possible rather than cluster (the result that undercuts Hotelling's own).

whyItMatters: It offers a tidy explanation for why competitors so often look alike and cluster together, from shops to political platforms to television schedules. Even after its formal foundation was shaken, the clustering intuition remains a widely used lens on competition and convergence.

working.lead: Expect convergence where buyers pick the nearest option
working.text: when customers choose the closest rival on some dimension, competitors are pulled toward each other's positions rather than apart.

working.lead: Treat it as a tendency, not a theorem
working.text: the clustering result is model-dependent; under different cost and competition assumptions firms may separate instead, so do not rely on it as a law.
the force pushing firms apart is the desire to avoid head-to-head price wars; where that dominates, expect differentiation, not clustering.

limits: Hotelling's clustering result is contested and not robust. In 1979 d'Aspremont, Gabszewicz and Thisse showed his original model is flawed: with linear transport costs no price equilibrium exists when the firms are close together, so the agglomeration-at-the-centre conclusion does not hold, and that in a repaired model with quadratic costs firms instead maximise differentiation, moving to opposite ends to soften price competition. So depending on the assumptions, competitors may cluster or separate; 'Hotelling's law' is better read as a suggestive, model-dependent tendency than a law.
misreadings: It is not an iron rule that competitors always converge: later, sounder models show they often maximise differentiation instead. It is an influential intuition about one force in competition (the pull toward shared customers), not a settled result.
origin: Introduced by the economist Harold Hotelling in his 1929 paper 'Stability in Competition' (The Economic Journal), which modelled competitors on a line and argued they tend to cluster; the label 'principle of minimum differentiation' is generally credited to Kenneth Boulding. The clustering claim was later shown defective by d'Aspremont, Gabszewicz and Thisse in 1979.

sources.text: Hotelling, H. (1929). "Stability in Competition." The Economic Journal, 39(153), 41–57.
